days.title: Structured, Semi-Structured, and Unstructured Data and File Formats

concepts.heading: Entities, Attributes, and Structured Data
concepts.body: Data is a collection of facts, such as numbers, descriptions and observations, that an organization records about things that matter to it. Those things are called entities, for example customers, products and sales orders, and each entity has attributes such as a name, an address or a price. Structured data follows a fixed schema, so every instance of an entity has the same fields. The usual shape is a table: each row is one instance of the entity and each column is one attribute. For example, a Product table where every row has ProductID, Name, Category and Price is structured data. Because every row looks the same, structured data is easy to validate, sort and total, and it is usually kept in a relational database where tables refer to each other through key values. On the exam, a fixed schema with rows and columns means structured data.

concepts.heading: Semi-Structured Data
concepts.body: Semi-structured data has some structure, but it allows variation between instances. A common example is a set of JSON documents describing customers: most customers have one email address, some have several, and some have none, and one customer document may include a field such as a unit number that another document leaves out. Each document still carries its own field names, so a program can read it, but there is no single schema that every record must match. This makes semi-structured data a good fit when records change over time, for example when a new device version starts sending an extra field. JSON is the format most often shown, but XML and other tagged or key-value formats are also semi-structured. If a question describes records that share a general shape but differ in which fields they contain, or that nest objects and lists, the answer is semi-structured data.

concepts.heading: Unstructured Data
concepts.body: Unstructured data has no specific field-and-value structure that a program can read directly. Documents, images, audio, video and other binary files are the classic examples: a scanned contract, a recorded phone call or a product photo. The content is still valuable, but to search or analyse it an application has to interpret it, for example by extracting text or recognizing objects. Unstructured files are usually kept as objects in a store such as Azure Blob Storage, often with a little metadata attached, such as a file name or upload date. Learn also mentions vector data, also called embeddings: numerical representations of text or images that AI applications compare to find content with a similar meaning. When a scenario lists photos, recordings, videos or free-form documents, think unstructured data; when it lists rows with identical columns, think structured; and when it lists JSON or XML with optional fields, think semi-structured.

concepts.heading: Human-Readable File Formats: CSV, JSON, and XML
concepts.body: Data is often stored in files, and the right format depends on the kind of data, the applications that read it and whether people need to read it. Delimited text is the simplest: in comma-separated values (CSV) each field is separated by a comma, each row ends with a new line, and the first line can hold the field names. Tab-separated and fixed-width text are close relatives. Delimited text suits structured data that many tools must open. JSON uses a hierarchical document schema: objects are enclosed in braces, collections in square brackets, and attributes are written as name and value pairs, so it handles both structured and semi-structured data. XML uses tags in angle brackets, such as Customer and Contact elements, to describe elements and attributes; it was popular in the 1990s and 2000s and has largely been replaced by the less verbose JSON, though some older systems still use it.

concepts.heading: Binary and Optimized Formats: BLOB, Parquet, Avro, and Delta Lake
concepts.body: All files are ultimately bytes, but some formats store raw binary data that an application must interpret and render, such as images, video, audio and application-specific documents. Data professionals call these files BLOBs, binary large objects. Human-readable formats are convenient but not optimized for space or processing, so specialized formats add compression and efficient reading. Parquet, an Apache project, is a columnar format widely used in data lakes and lakehouses: values for each column are stored together in row groups, and metadata lets a reader fetch only the columns and rows it needs. Avro, also an Apache project, is row-based: each file has a JSON header that describes the structure, followed by binary blocks of records, which makes it compact for storage and network transfer. Delta Lake, an open-source storage format, builds on Parquet by adding a transaction log, which enables ACID transactions and data versioning on files in a data lake.

examPoints: A question that describes rows with the same columns is testing structured data, one with JSON or XML records whose fields vary is testing semi-structured data, and one with images, audio, video or documents is testing unstructured data.

A question about a human-readable format that almost any tool can open for tabular data points to CSV, while one about nested objects in braces and lists in square brackets points to JSON, and angle-bracket tags point to XML.

A question about reading only a few columns of a very wide table in a data lake points to a columnar format such as Parquet, while one about a compact row-based format with a JSON header describing the schema points to Avro.

quiz.q: A smart-home app stores each device's settings as a JSON document. A thermostat document has temperature fields, while a door lock document has a lock state and no temperature at all. How is this data best classified?
choices: Structured data, because every JSON document is converted into the same table row
Semi-structured data, because each document has named fields that vary by device
Unstructured data, because JSON documents are stored as binary objects in a file
Vector data, because each document is a numerical representation of its meaning
quiz.explain: JSON documents carry their own field names but allow the fields to differ between records, which is semi-structured data. Choice A is tempting because the data does have fields, but structured data needs a fixed schema where every record has the same fields.

quiz.q: A data team stores years of web events in a data lake. Most reports read three columns out of more than a hundred, over billions of rows. Which file format best suits this read pattern?
choices: CSV, because a header line names every column and any tool can open the file
XML, because tags around each element let a reader skip unwanted attributes
Avro, because a JSON header describes the schema of every binary record block
Parquet, because values for each column are stored together with metadata
quiz.explain: Parquet is columnar, so a query can read only the columns it needs and skip the rest, which suits wide tables with narrow queries. Choice C is tempting because Avro is also an optimized binary format, but it is row-based and reads whole records.

days.recap: Data is structured (fixed schema in rows and columns), semi-structured (JSON or XML with fields that vary) or unstructured (images, audio, video, documents), and it is stored in human-readable files such as CSV, JSON and XML or in optimized formats such as columnar Parquet and row-based Avro.

days.title: Data Store Types and Choosing an Azure Data Store

concepts.heading: File Stores and Databases
concepts.body: Organizations keep data in two broad kinds of store. A file store holds whole files, such as CSV exports, JSON documents, Parquet files, images and videos, in a shared location, increasingly in the cloud. A database is a dedicated system for managing data records rather than files: it stores records, lets you query them and protects them while many users read and write at once. Databases split into two families. Relational databases store structured data in tables and use SQL to query them. Nonrelational databases, often called NoSQL databases, do not apply a relational schema; the name is loose, because some of them support a variant of SQL. Choosing a store starts with the shape of the data and how it will be used: rows that must stay consistent, documents with flexible fields, values looked up by a key, relationships between things, or large files written once and read many times.

concepts.heading: Relational Databases
concepts.body: A relational database stores data in tables that represent entities, such as Customer, Product and Order. Each row is given a primary key that uniquely identifies it, and other tables refer to that row by storing the key as a foreign key. For example, an Order row stores the customer's ID instead of repeating the customer's name and address, so each customer's details are stored only once. This use of keys lets the database be normalized and lets it enforce rules such as rejecting an order for a customer that does not exist. Tables are created and queried with Structured Query Language (SQL), which is based on an ANSI standard and is similar across database systems. Relational stores are the usual choice for transactional business data such as orders, payments and inventory, where the structure is known in advance and data must stay correct when many changes happen at the same time.

concepts.heading: Key-Value and Document Databases
concepts.body: A key-value database stores each record as a unique key and an associated value, and the value can be in any format. Most key-value stores support only simple query, insert and delete operations by key, so finding records by something inside the value means redesigning the data. That makes key-value stores a good fit for lookups such as a user's session data or a shopping cart retrieved by session ID. A document database is a specific form of key-value database in which the value is a JSON document that the system is optimized to parse and query. Because the database understands the fields inside each document, you can query by any field, such as all customers in a given city, and different documents can have different fields. Document databases suit catalogs, user profiles and content where each item's shape varies and the whole item is usually read and written together.

concepts.heading: Column-Family, Graph, and Object Stores
concepts.body: A column-family database stores tabular data in rows and columns, but the columns are divided into groups called column families, each holding columns that are logically related and usually read together. It suits very wide, sparse data with heavy writes, such as readings from millions of sensors; Apache Cassandra is a well-known example. A graph database stores entities as nodes and the relationships between them as links, called edges, so it can follow chains of connections quickly, for example friends of friends in a social network or accounts linked through shared phone numbers in fraud detection. An object store keeps unstructured files, such as images, videos and backups, as objects with metadata and serves them over HTTP; in Azure this is Azure Blob Storage. When a question stresses relationships several hops apart, think graph; when it stresses wide rows with groups of related columns, think column-family; when it stresses large files, think object storage.

concepts.heading: Matching Common Use Cases to Azure Data Stores
concepts.body: At the fundamentals level, the exam asks you to match a need to a type of Azure store. For relational, transactional data choose an Azure relational service: Azure SQL Database or SQL Managed Instance for SQL Server workloads, or Azure Database for PostgreSQL or Azure Database for MySQL for those open-source engines. For document, key-value, column-family or graph data that needs low latency and global scale, choose Azure Cosmos DB, which offers several APIs, including NoSQL and MongoDB for documents, Apache Cassandra for column-family data, Apache Gremlin for graphs and Table for key-value data. For images, video, backups and other unstructured files choose Azure Blob Storage; Azure Data Lake Storage builds on it with a hierarchical namespace for analytics files. Azure Files provides file shares that servers can mount, and Azure Table Storage is a schemaless key/attribute store for structured NoSQL data. Later days cover each of these services in more detail.

examPoints: A question about values found only by a unique key, such as session data, is testing a key-value store, while one about querying fields inside JSON items whose shape varies is testing a document database.

A question about finding connections several links apart, such as fraud rings or social networks, points to a graph database, and one about very wide, sparse rows with groups of related columns points to a column-family database.

A question that needs consistent transactions over related tables points to an Azure relational service, one about storing photos, videos or backups points to Azure Blob Storage, and one about document, key-value, column-family or graph data at global scale points to Azure Cosmos DB.

quiz.q: A recipe website lets users store recipes. Some recipes include a list of ingredients and a video link, others add nutrition facts, and the site must search recipes by any field. Which type of data store fits best?
choices: A key-value store, because each recipe can be looked up quickly by its recipe ID
A graph database, because each ingredient links to other recipes as nodes and edges
A document database, because it parses JSON items whose fields vary and queries them
A column-family database, because related columns such as nutrition facts form a group
quiz.explain: A document database understands the JSON inside each item, so recipes with different fields can be stored together and searched by any field. Choice A is tempting because recipes have IDs, but most key-value stores support only simple lookups by key, not queries on fields inside the value.

quiz.q: A museum is digitizing its collection and must store millions of high-resolution photos and audio guides that are written once and then downloaded by visitors' browsers. Which Azure service is the natural choice?
choices: Azure Blob Storage, which stores unstructured files as objects served over HTTP
Azure SQL Database, which stores each photo in a table column with a primary key
Azure Table Storage, which stores each photo as a value found by its partition key
Azure Cosmos DB for Apache Gremlin, which stores each photo as a node in a graph
quiz.explain: Photos and audio are unstructured binary files, and Azure Blob Storage is Azure's object store for them. Choice B is tempting because a relational database can hold binary columns, but it is built for structured rows, not millions of large media files.

days.recap: Data stores are file stores or databases, and databases are relational (tables, keys, SQL) or nonrelational (key-value, document, column-family, graph), while object storage holds unstructured files; in Azure that maps to the relational services, Azure Cosmos DB and Azure Blob Storage.

days.title: Transactional and Analytical Data Workloads

concepts.heading: Transactional Workloads (OLTP)
concepts.body: A transactional system records transactions, which are small, discrete units of work that capture an event the business wants to track: a payment, a seat booking, a stock movement or a transfer between bank accounts. This work is called online transactional processing (OLTP). OLTP systems are often high volume, sometimes handling millions of transactions a day, and the data must be available quickly. The database is optimized for both reading and writing, because applications constantly create, retrieve, update and delete records, often called CRUD operations. The data is usually normalized into many related tables so each fact is stored once and stays correct. OLTP databases sit behind live line-of-business applications such as point-of-sale, order entry and banking apps. In a question, many small reads and writes from an application, with each change needing to be exact, describe a transactional workload.

concepts.heading: ACID: How Transactions Stay Correct
concepts.body: OLTP databases enforce transactions with ACID semantics. Take a transfer of 40 from account A to account B. Atomicity: the transaction is a single unit that succeeds completely or fails completely, so if the credit to B cannot be written, the debit from A is undone too. Consistency: a transaction can move the database only from one valid state to another, so the money leaves A and arrives in B and the totals still add up. Isolation: concurrent transactions cannot interfere with each other, so a query that checks both balances during the transfer never sees A after the transfer and B before it. Durability: once a transaction is committed it stays committed, so the new balances survive even if the server loses power a moment later. Exam questions often describe one of these behaviours in a story and ask which property it is; match the story to the single word.

concepts.heading: Analytical Workloads (OLAP)
concepts.body: Analytical processing uses read-only or read-mostly systems that hold large volumes of historical data or business metrics, so people can find trends and make decisions. A common architecture copies operational data out of OLTP systems through extract, transform and load (ETL), or extract and load first and transform later (ELT), into an analytical store. There the data is shaped for reading, often with some denormalization, which repeats values to make queries faster. It may then be aggregated into an online analytical processing (OLAP) model, today usually called a semantic model and historically a cube, where measures such as sales revenue are pre-calculated across dimensions such as date, region and product. Because the totals are pre-aggregated, users can drill up and down from region to city to store and get answers quickly. Running heavy reports directly on the OLTP database instead can slow down the application.

concepts.heading: Data Warehouse, Data Lake, and Lakehouse
concepts.body: A data warehouse stores data in a relational schema that is optimized for read operations, mainly queries for reporting and visualization. Data is cleaned and structured before it is loaded, so analysts get consistent results with SQL. A data lake is a store for large volumes of file-based data in many formats, such as CSV, JSON, Parquet, logs and images, kept in its raw form at low cost so data scientists can decide later how to use it; structure is applied when the data is read, an approach Learn calls schema-on-read. A data lakehouse is a newer pattern that combines the flexible, scalable storage of a data lake with the relational querying of a warehouse, by placing table definitions over files in the lake. In Azure, Microsoft Fabric provides lakehouse and warehouse items in one SaaS platform, and Azure Databricks, built on Apache Spark, uses Delta Lake as its native table format.

concepts.heading: Batch and Interactive Analysis
concepts.body: Analytical work is often processed in batches: a scheduled job collects a large set of data, such as all of the day's sales files, processes it in one run and writes results that reports use the next morning. Batch processing is efficient for large volumes and complex transformations, but the results are only as fresh as the last run. Interactive analysis is different: a person asks ad hoc questions, adjusts a query or a notebook cell, and sees results within the session. Data scientists often explore raw lake files this way in notebooks with Python or SQL, using Apache Spark in Azure Databricks or Microsoft Fabric, and analysts slice a semantic model in Power BI. A third pattern, stream processing, handles each event as it arrives and is covered on a later day. If a scenario says nightly or scheduled over a large set, think batch; if it says ad hoc, exploring or iterating, think interactive.

examPoints: A question about many small inserts and updates from a live application, with normalized tables and exact results, is testing a transactional (OLTP) workload, while one about trends over years of history is testing an analytical workload.
A question that describes all-or-nothing changes, other queries never seeing half-finished work, or committed data surviving a power cut is testing atomicity, isolation and durability respectively.

A question about cleaned, structured data queried with SQL for consistent reports points to a data warehouse, while one about raw files of many formats kept cheaply for later use points to a data lake.

quiz.q: A bank's mobile app shows a customer's balance. While a transfer is being written, the app must never display a total that mixes the old balance of one account with the new balance of another. Which ACID property ensures this?
choices: Atomicity, because the debit and the credit either both complete or both roll back
Durability, because committed balances remain stored even after a server restart
Consistency, because each transaction leaves the account totals in a valid state
Isolation, because concurrent transactions cannot see each other's partial changes
quiz.explain: Isolation keeps a concurrent read from seeing a transaction that is only half done. Choice A is tempting because the transfer is all or nothing, but atomicity is about the transfer itself completing or failing, not what other queries see meanwhile.

quiz.q: A clothing retailer wants leaders to compare sales by store, product line and quarter for the past six years, without slowing the checkout database. What is the usual approach?
choices: Add more indexes to the checkout database so that the long reports finish faster
Copy the data into an analytical store and pre-aggregate it in a semantic model
Run the reports on the checkout database only during busy trading hours each day
Store each sale as an unstructured file so the reports can read it as raw binary
quiz.explain: Copying history out of the OLTP system into an analytical store, often with a pre-aggregated semantic model, gives fast trend reports without loading the transactional database. Choice A is tempting, but extra indexes slow down every write in a busy checkout system.

days.recap: Transactional (OLTP) workloads run many small, ACID-protected reads and writes for live applications, while analytical workloads copy history into data warehouses, data lakes or lakehouses and semantic models, processed in batches or explored interactively.

days.title: Data Roles: Database Administrator, Data Engineer, and Data Analyst

concepts.heading: Why the Exam Separates Data Roles
concepts.body: Many people work with data, and the exam expects you to know who usually does what. The three roles in the skills list are the database administrator, the data engineer and the data analyst. A useful way to remember them is to follow the data: the database administrator keeps the operational databases running and secure, the data engineer moves and prepares data for analysis, and the data analyst turns prepared data into insight. Organizations define roles differently, and one person can hold several. For example, someone might provision an Azure SQL Database as a database administrator and later build a pipeline that copies its data into a warehouse as a data engineer. Note: the Learn module now also lists an AI engineer, who builds AI features with large language models in Microsoft Foundry, and mentions data scientists and data architects, but the skills list names only the three roles above.

concepts.heading: Database Administrator
concepts.body: A database administrator (DBA) is responsible for the design, implementation, maintenance and operation of database systems, on premises and in the cloud. The DBA looks after the availability and consistent performance of the databases, tunes them when queries slow down, and works with stakeholders on backup and recovery plans so data can be restored after a hardware failure, a disaster or a user deleting rows by mistake. The DBA also manages security: creating logins, granting or denying access to users as appropriate, and removing access that is no longer needed. In Azure, a DBA typically works with Azure SQL Database, Azure SQL Managed Instance, SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines, and Azure Database for PostgreSQL and MySQL, using tools such as the Azure portal and SQL client tools. If a question mentions permissions, backups, restores, uptime or database performance tuning, the answer is the database administrator.

concepts.heading: Data Engineer
concepts.body: A data engineer designs and implements data workloads with stakeholders: data ingestion pipelines, cleansing and transformation steps, and the data stores used for analytics, such as warehouse and lakehouse tables. Data engineers work with a wide range of platforms, including relational and nonrelational databases, file stores and data streams. They are also responsible for keeping data private as it moves from on-premises systems to cloud stores, and they own the management and monitoring of pipelines, so a nightly load that fails or finishes late is their problem to fix. A typical example is combining CRM, ERP and web log data every night, removing duplicates and standardizing dates, then loading it into an analytical store. In Azure, data engineers commonly use Microsoft Fabric (Data Factory pipelines, lakehouses and warehouses), Azure Databricks, Azure Data Lake Storage and Azure Cosmos DB.

concepts.heading: Data Analyst
concepts.body: A data analyst helps a business get the most value from its data. Analysts explore data to find trends and relationships, design and build analytical models, and share findings through reports and visualizations so leaders can make informed decisions. They usually start from data that engineers have already cleaned and loaded, then define measures, relationships and visuals that answer business questions, such as which products are growing in each region. The tool most associated with this role on the exam is Power BI, which connects to data, builds semantic models and publishes interactive reports and dashboards; analysts may also query warehouse tables in Microsoft Fabric with SQL. AI assistants such as Copilot can suggest visuals or summarize reports, but the business understanding and the communication of results stay with the analyst. If a question is about charts, dashboards, report design or finding trends for decision makers, the answer is the data analyst.

concepts.heading: Telling the Roles Apart in Scenarios
concepts.body: Exam questions usually describe a task and ask which role owns it, so look for the verb and the object. Keeping a database secure, available, backed up and fast belongs to the database administrator: grant read access to a new application, restore a deleted table, or investigate slow queries at peak time. Moving, cleaning and loading data, and keeping pipelines healthy, belongs to the data engineer: ingest files nightly, fix a load that failed without warning, or design the warehouse tables the pipelines fill. Exploring prepared data and presenting it belongs to the data analyst: build a sales trend report, create a dashboard for managers, or define a measure for profit margin. Watch for distractors that swap neighbouring tasks; designing the analytical data store is the engineer's job even though the analyst uses it, and granting permissions is the DBA's job even when the data feeds a report.

examPoints: A question about granting or removing user access, planning backups and restores, or keeping a database available and fast is testing the database administrator role.
A question about building and monitoring pipelines that ingest, clean and transform data, or designing analytical data stores, is testing the data engineer role.
A question about exploring curated data for trends and building reports and dashboards, usually in Power BI, is testing the data analyst role.

quiz.q: After a merger, sales data from two companies uses different product codes and date formats. Someone must build a repeatable process that standardizes the codes and dates and loads the result into the lakehouse every night. Which role typically does this?
choices: A data engineer, who builds and runs pipelines that clean and load the data
A data analyst, who builds reports that compare sales across both companies
A database administrator, who grants access to both companies' sales tables
A business user, who reads the pre-aggregated totals in a shared dashboard
quiz.explain: Building repeatable ingestion and cleansing pipelines into an analytical store is the data engineer's job. Choice B is tempting because the analyst will use the merged data, but the analyst works on data after the engineer has prepared it.

quiz.q: A regional manager wants a visual that shows each store's monthly returns against its sales, with a filter by product category, built on data already in the warehouse. Which role and tool fit this request?
choices: A database administrator using SQL client tools to tune the warehouse indexes
A data engineer using a Data Factory pipeline to copy the warehouse into a lake
A data analyst using Power BI to model the data and build an interactive report
An AI engineer using Microsoft Foundry to deploy a language model over the data
quiz.explain: Turning curated warehouse data into interactive visuals for decision makers is the data analyst's work, typically in Power BI. Choice B is tempting because Fabric pipelines move warehouse data, but the data is already loaded and the request is for a report.

days.recap: Database administrators keep databases secure, available, backed up and fast; data engineers build and monitor the pipelines and analytical stores that prepare data; and data analysts explore that data and present it in reports and dashboards, mostly with Power BI.

days.title: Relational Concepts: Tables, Keys, and Normalization

concepts.heading: Tables, Rows, Columns, and Data Types
concepts.body: In a relational database, each kind of entity, such as Customer, Product or Order, is stored in its own table. A table is made of rows and columns: each row represents one instance of the entity, for example one customer, and each column represents one attribute, for example FirstName or City. Every column has a data type that constrains what it can hold, such as INT for whole numbers, DECIMAL for prices and VARCHAR for variable-length text. A column can be marked NOT NULL, which makes it mandatory, or it can allow NULL, which means a row may have no value there, for example when a customer has no middle name. Because every row in a table has the same columns, relational data is structured data with a fixed schema. Adding a new attribute later means changing the table definition so the new column exists for every row, even if many rows leave it empty.

concepts.heading: Primary Keys
concepts.body: Each row in a table should be uniquely identified by a primary key. Most often this is a single ID column, such as CustomerID or ProductID, but it can be any column or set of columns whose value is different for every row. The database enforces the primary key: it rejects a new row that repeats an existing key value, and it does not allow the key to be empty. SQL does not force every table to have a primary key, but good design gives each table one. When no single column is unique, a composite key combines several columns. For example, in an OrderLine table the OrderNo repeats for every item on an order and the ItemNo repeats across orders, but each pair of OrderNo and ItemNo occurs only once, so the two columns together form the key. On the exam, the column that uniquely identifies a row and can never be repeated or empty is the primary key.

concepts.heading: Foreign Keys and Referential Integrity
concepts.body: Tables are related by storing one table's primary key in another table, where it is called a foreign key. For example, the Order table has a CustomerID column that holds the ID of the customer who placed the order. The customer's name and address stay in the Customer table, and any query can look them up through that link. A relational database management system can enforce referential integrity on this relationship: it checks that every value placed in a foreign key column matches an existing primary key in the related table. If an application tries to insert an order for customer 950 and no customer 950 exists, the database rejects the row, so there are no orphaned orders for customers who are not on file. Foreign keys are also what queries use to join tables back together. In a question, a column that refers to another table's primary key, or a rule that rejects references to missing rows, is about foreign keys.

concepts.heading: Normalization: What It Is
concepts.body: Normalization is the schema design process that minimizes duplicate data and enforces data integrity. Formal normal forms exist, but Learn gives a practical definition with four rules: separate each entity into its own table, separate each discrete attribute into its own column, uniquely identify each row with a primary key, and use foreign key columns to link related entities. Picture a sales spreadsheet in which every line repeats the customer's name and address and the product's name and price, and a single cell holds a full name and street address together. Normalizing it produces Customer, Product, Order and LineItem tables. Each customer appears in one row of Customer, each product in one row of Product, and each line item refers to them by key. Each attribute, such as City or UnitPrice, gets its own column with a suitable data type, so prices must be decimal and quantities must be whole numbers.

concepts.heading: Why Normalize, and When Not To
concepts.body: Normalization brings three practical benefits. First, it removes duplication: when a customer moves, you change the address in one row instead of dozens, so different rows can never disagree. Second, separate columns with proper data types protect quality and make querying easy, for example filtering customers by City, which is hard when the city is buried inside a longer text cell. Third, keys and referential integrity stop invalid data, such as an order for a product that does not exist. These benefits suit transactional systems, where data changes constantly and must stay correct. The cost is that queries often have to join several tables to rebuild a complete picture. Analytical stores therefore often denormalize: they combine tables and repeat values such as product names on many rows so that read-heavy reports run faster. On the exam, normalization is for consistent OLTP data and denormalization for faster analytical reads.

examPoints: A question about a column that uniquely identifies each row and rejects repeated or empty values is testing the primary key, and one where two columns together are unique is testing a composite key.
A question in which the database rejects a row that refers to a missing customer or product is testing a foreign key enforcing referential integrity.

A question about the same address repeated on many rows, updates missed in some rows, or several values crammed into one cell is testing why normalization is used: one entity per table, one attribute per column.

quiz.q: A school's database has a Student table with the primary key StudentID and an Enrollment table that records which course each student takes. How should the Enrollment table record the student?
choices: Copy the student's full name and home address into every enrollment row
Store the StudentID in a foreign key column that refers to the Student table
Store the student's details in a JSON document inside one enrollment column
Create a new primary key in Student for every course that the student takes
quiz.explain: A foreign key column holding StudentID links each enrollment to exactly one student while the student's details stay in one place. Choice A is tempting because it makes each row complete, but it duplicates data and causes inconsistent updates, which normalization avoids.

quiz.q: A small clinic stores appointments in one sheet where each row holds a cell like "Dr Lee, Cardiology, Room 4". Staff cannot list all cardiology appointments easily, and a doctor's room change must be edited on many rows. What should a normalized design do?
choices: Keep one table and add an index on the combined cell that holds each doctor's details
Store each appointment as a separate unstructured text file in a shared file store
Add a second copy of the sheet that is sorted by department for quicker cardiology lookups
Put doctors in their own table, one column per attribute, linked to appointments by key
quiz.explain: Normalization gives the doctor entity its own table, splits each attribute into its own column, and links appointments by key, so a room change is made once and departments can be filtered. Choice A is tempting, but an index speeds lookups without fixing the combined values or the duplication.

days.recap: Relational data lives in tables of rows and typed columns, rows are identified by primary keys and linked by foreign keys with referential integrity, and normalization puts each entity in its own table and each attribute in its own column to remove duplication, while analytics often denormalizes for speed.

days.title: SQL Statements and Database Objects

concepts.heading: SQL and Its Dialects
concepts.body: SQL, Structured Query Language, is the standard language for relational database management systems. It was standardized by ANSI in 1986 and by ISO in 1987, so statements such as SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, CREATE and DROP look much the same in every system. Vendors also add their own extensions for areas such as stored procedure code, triggers and security, which has produced several dialects. Transact-SQL (T-SQL) is used by Microsoft SQL Server, Azure SQL Database, Azure SQL Managed Instance and SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines. PL/pgSQL is the procedural dialect of PostgreSQL, and PL/SQL is Oracle's. MySQL has its own variant too. This explains why procedural code written for an Azure SQL Database looks slightly different from code for Azure Database for PostgreSQL, even though basic queries are nearly identical. The exam does not test detailed syntax; it expects you to recognize short statements and know what they do.

concepts.heading: DDL and DCL: Defining Objects and Controlling Access
concepts.body: Learn groups SQL statements into three main logical groups: DDL, DCL and DML. Data Definition Language (DDL) creates, changes and removes database objects such as tables, views and stored procedures. CREATE makes a new object, ALTER changes its structure, for example adding a column to a table that already holds rows, DROP removes the object, and RENAME renames it. DROP is permanent: dropping a table removes all of its rows, so they are gone unless you have a backup. A short example is `CREATE TABLE Product (ID INT PRIMARY KEY, Name VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL, Price DECIMAL NULL);`, which creates a table with a mandatory Name and an optional Price. Data Control Language (DCL) manages permissions and is mainly used by database administrators. GRANT gives a user or group permission to perform actions, DENY explicitly blocks them, and REVOKE removes a permission granted earlier. For example, `GRANT SELECT, INSERT ON Product TO user1;` lets user1 read and add rows.

concepts.heading: DML and Queries: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE
concepts.body: Data Manipulation Language (DML) works with the rows inside tables. Learn lists four main DML statements: SELECT reads rows, INSERT adds rows, UPDATE changes values in existing rows and DELETE removes rows. Learn puts SELECT under DML; some other courses give it a separate label, Data Query Language (DQL), which is only an alternative name for the same statement. A WHERE clause limits which rows are affected, as in `SELECT FirstName, City FROM Customer WHERE City = 'Seattle' ORDER BY LastName;`, where ORDER BY sorts the results, because rows otherwise come back in no guaranteed order. SQL never asks whether you are sure. `UPDATE Customer SET Address = '123 High St.' WHERE ID = 1;` changes one customer, but the same statement without WHERE changes every row, and `DELETE FROM Product` without WHERE empties the table while keeping its structure. INSERT names the table and columns and supplies values, as in `INSERT INTO Product (ID, Name, Price) VALUES (99, 'Drill', 4.99);`.

concepts.heading: Joining Tables
concepts.body: Because normalized data is spread across tables, queries combine them with a JOIN clause, which says how rows in one table match rows in another. The usual join condition matches a foreign key with its primary key, for example `SELECT o.OrderNo, c.City FROM [Order] AS o JOIN Customer AS c ON o.CustomerID = c.ID;`. The short names o and c are table aliases, and ORDER is in square brackets because it is a reserved word in T-SQL. A plain JOIN is an inner join: it returns only rows that have a match in both tables, so customers with no orders are left out. A LEFT OUTER JOIN keeps every row from the left table and fills the right side with NULL where no match exists, which lists every customer, including those who have never ordered. RIGHT OUTER JOIN does the same for the right table, and FULL OUTER JOIN keeps unmatched rows from both. Recognize joins by the ON clause that pairs key columns.

concepts.heading: Views, Stored Procedures, and Indexes
concepts.body: A relational database holds other objects besides tables. A view is a virtual table based on the results of a SELECT query; it stores the query, not a copy of the data. A view named Deliveries could join Order and Customer once, so analysts can simply query `SELECT * FROM Deliveries WHERE City = 'Seattle';` without writing the join. A stored procedure is a named set of SQL statements kept in the database and run on command, often with parameters. For example, `EXEC RenameProduct 201, 'Spanner';` runs one shared piece of update logic that every application can call. An index works like the index at the back of a book: it keeps a sorted copy of one or more columns with pointers to the rows, so a query filtering on that column can avoid scanning the whole table, as created by `CREATE INDEX idx_ProductName ON Product(Name);`. Indexes cost storage and slow down inserts, updates and deletes, because every index must be maintained.

examPoints: A question listing CREATE, ALTER, DROP or RENAME is testing DDL, one listing GRANT, DENY or REVOKE is testing DCL, and one listing SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE is testing DML (Learn puts SELECT under DML; DQL is only an alternative label used elsewhere).

A question about an UPDATE or DELETE that changed every row is testing a missing WHERE clause, and one that must keep unmatched rows from one table, such as customers with no orders, is testing an outer join.

A question about saving a query as a virtual table points to a view, reusable logic with parameters points to a stored procedure, and faster lookups on a column at the cost of slower writes points to an index.

quiz.q: A team wants to add an optional Discontinued column to an existing Product table that already holds thousands of rows, keeping all of the current data. Which statement should they use?
choices: ALTER TABLE, a DDL statement that changes the structure of an existing table
UPDATE, a DML statement that changes the values held in the existing rows
DROP TABLE followed by CREATE TABLE, two DDL statements that rebuild it
GRANT, a DCL statement that gives users permission to use the new column
quiz.explain: ALTER TABLE changes an object's structure, such as adding a column, without losing the existing rows. Choice B is tempting because the rows change too, but UPDATE can only set values in columns that already exist; it cannot add a column.

quiz.q: Report writers keep repeating the same three-table join to list orders with customer names and product names. The DBA wants one object they can query like a table, without storing a second copy of the data. What should the DBA create?
choices: A stored procedure that copies the joined rows into a new table every night
An index on the customer name column so that the three-table join runs faster
A view whose SELECT statement joins the three tables for the report writers
A new table that repeats the customer and product names on every order row
quiz.explain: A view is a virtual table defined by a SELECT query, so report writers can query it like a table while the data stays in the base tables. Choice A is tempting because procedures package logic, but copying rows into a new table stores a second copy of the data.

days.recap: SQL groups statements into DDL (CREATE, ALTER, DROP), DCL (GRANT, DENY, REVOKE) and DML (SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, with Learn placing SELECT under DML and DQL only an alternative label), joins tables on key columns, and adds views, stored procedures and indexes to simplify queries, reuse logic and speed up lookups.

days.title: Relational Database Services on Azure
services: SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines

concepts.heading: IaaS and PaaS for Databases
concepts.body: Azure offers relational databases at two levels of management. With infrastructure as a service (IaaS) you get a virtual machine and install and run the database engine yourself, so you control everything but also patch the operating system and the database, configure backups and handle maintenance. With platform as a service (PaaS) Microsoft runs the server, the operating system and the database engine, and provides automated updates, backups and high availability, while you manage your data, schema, users and access. The trade-off is control against effort: PaaS removes most administration but hides the operating system and some instance-level features, while IaaS keeps full control for workloads that need it. Azure SQL is the collective name for three SQL Server-based services: SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines (IaaS), Azure SQL Managed Instance (PaaS) and Azure SQL Database (PaaS). Azure also offers PaaS services for the open-source PostgreSQL and MySQL engines.

concepts.heading: Azure SQL Database: Single Database and Elastic Pool
concepts.body: Azure SQL Database is a fully managed, highly scalable PaaS database service designed for the cloud. It includes the core database-level features of SQL Server and is the usual choice for a new cloud application, or for migrating applications that have few instance-level dependencies. Microsoft handles patching, backups and high availability. You can deploy a single database, which has its own dedicated resources and is managed through a logical server, a connection and administration point for one or more databases. Or you can use an elastic pool, where many databases share a set of resources. Pools suit software-as-a-service vendors that give each customer a separate database: most databases are quiet most of the time and peak at different moments, so sharing resources is more efficient than sizing each one for its own peak. Some on-premises features, such as SQL Server Agent jobs, cross-database queries and linked servers, are not available in SQL Database.

concepts.heading: Azure SQL Managed Instance
concepts.body: Azure SQL Managed Instance is a PaaS option that runs a full SQL Server instance in the cloud with near-100% compatibility with on-premises SQL Server. You can create multiple databases on the same instance and keep instance-level features that Azure SQL Database lacks, such as SQL Server Agent, cross-database queries and linked servers, so most on-premises databases move with minimal code changes. Microsoft still automates backups, patching and monitoring, while you control security and resource allocation for your databases. A managed instance is deployed into your own Azure virtual network, so it uses private IP addresses and can reach on-premises networks over a VPN or ExpressRoute connection. This makes it the usual answer for lift-and-shift migrations of whole SQL Server instances when the company wants to stop managing servers. The Azure Database Migration Service can help move databases to it, and an Azure SQL assessment, run with Azure Migrate or SQL Server enabled by Azure Arc, reports whether instances are ready to migrate.

concepts.heading: SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines
concepts.body: SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines is SQL Server installed on a Windows or Linux virtual machine in Azure, which makes it IaaS. It is fully compatible with on-premises SQL Server, so applications and databases can be lifted and shifted without changes, and you have full administrative rights over the operating system and the database engine. That matters when software must be installed on the same server as SQL Server, when the application needs operating system features that PaaS hides, or when the team must keep exact control of configuration. You can also resize the VM to give SQL Server more memory, CPU or disk without reinstalling the software, and use VMs for development, testing or hybrid deployments. The cost of that control is responsibility: you manage operating system and SQL Server updates, configuration and backups. The VM's availability commitment covers the virtual machine, not the SQL Server service running on it.

concepts.heading: Azure Database for PostgreSQL and MySQL
concepts.body: For open-source engines, Azure offers Azure Database for PostgreSQL and Azure Database for MySQL, both deployed as flexible server, a fully managed PaaS service with granular control over configuration, maintenance windows and cost options. They let organizations move existing PostgreSQL or MySQL apps to Azure without significant changes. Azure Database for MySQL is based on MySQL Community Edition and is a common choice for LAMP-stack web apps (Linux, Apache, MySQL, PHP). PostgreSQL is an object-relational database: besides tables it supports custom data types, extensions and geometric data such as lines and polygons, and its procedural language is PL/pgSQL. Both services provide automatic backups with point-in-time restore, built-in high availability with automatic failover, firewall rules and TLS connections, monitoring and alerts. Some server-level tasks, such as running your own server backup and restore from pgAdmin, are unavailable because Microsoft manages the server. Azure Database for MariaDB is retired; Learn recommends migrating to Azure Database for MySQL, so MariaDB is never the answer for a new design.

examPoints: A question about a new cloud application that needs a managed SQL Server-based database points to Azure SQL Database, and one about many small databases with peaks at different times points to an elastic pool.

A question about moving a whole SQL Server instance with features such as SQL Server Agent, cross-database queries or linked servers to PaaS points to Azure SQL Managed Instance, while one that needs operating system access or full control points to SQL Server on Azure VMs.
A question about a managed service for existing open-source PostgreSQL or MySQL apps, such as a LAMP-stack site, points to Azure Database for PostgreSQL or MySQL flexible server.

quiz.q: A company is moving an on-premises SQL Server application to Azure. A third-party backup agent must run on the same server as SQL Server and needs administrator access to the operating system. Which service should it use?
choices: Azure SQL Database, because each single database has its own dedicated resources
Azure SQL Managed Instance, because it offers near-full SQL Server compatibility
Azure Database for MySQL flexible server, because it allows custom server settings
SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines, because it gives full control of the server OS
quiz.explain: Only SQL Server on Azure VMs, the IaaS option, gives access to the operating system so the agent can be installed beside SQL Server. Choice B is tempting because Managed Instance is highly compatible with SQL Server, but it is PaaS and hides the operating system.

quiz.q: A developer team runs PostgreSQL on premises with PL/pgSQL stored procedures and geometric data. It wants Microsoft to handle patching, backups and failover with minimal application changes. Which Azure service fits best?
choices: Azure SQL Database, migrating the procedures from PL/pgSQL to Transact-SQL code
Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server, a managed PaaS PostgreSQL service
SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines, installing PostgreSQL beside the database
Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL, storing each row as a JSON document in a container
quiz.explain: Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server runs the same engine as a managed PaaS service, so PL/pgSQL code and geometric types move with minimal change. Choice A is tempting because SQL Database is fully managed, but it runs the SQL Server engine and would require rewriting the code.

days.recap: Azure SQL covers SQL Server on Azure VMs (IaaS, full control), Azure SQL Managed Instance (PaaS, near-full instance compatibility) and Azure SQL Database (PaaS, single database or elastic pool for new cloud apps), and Azure Database for PostgreSQL and MySQL flexible server run the open-source engines as managed services.

days.title: Azure Storage: Blobs, Access Tiers, Data Lake Storage, Files, and Tables

concepts.heading: Storage Accounts and Blob Containers
concepts.body: An Azure storage account is the top-level namespace for several data services: Blob Storage for unstructured objects, Azure Files for file shares, Table storage for key-attribute data, and Queue storage for messages between application components. Inside Blob Storage, data is organized in three levels: the storage account, then containers, then blobs. A container groups blobs much like a folder, and each blob is one stored object, such as a photo, a video, a PDF or a backup file, with its own URL. That URL is why Blob Storage suits websites that serve images directly to browsers over HTTPS. For example, a retailer can keep millions of product photos in a container named images and let its online store link to each one. Blob Storage does not care what is inside a file, so it is the default answer for large volumes of unstructured data with no fixed schema.

concepts.heading: Block, Page, and Append Blobs
concepts.body: Blob Storage has three blob types, and the exam expects you to match each one to a workload. Block blobs are made of blocks that are uploaded and managed separately, which makes them the right choice for ordinary files such as documents, images, video and backups; they are the most common type. Page blobs are collections of fixed-size pages optimized for random read and write operations, which is exactly what the virtual hard disks of Azure virtual machines need. Append blobs are block blobs optimized for append operations: new blocks can be added only at the end, and existing blocks cannot be changed or removed. That makes append blobs a natural fit for logs and audit trails that only ever grow. A scenario that says a file is only ever added to at the end points to append blobs, and a scenario about VM disks points to page blobs.

concepts.heading: Hot, Cool, Cold, and Archive Tiers
concepts.body: Access tiers let you trade storage cost against access cost, and they apply only to block blobs. The hot tier is for data in active use: storage costs the most, but reading it costs the least. The cool tier is for infrequently accessed data kept at least 30 days, and the cold tier is for rarely accessed data kept at least 90 days; both are online, so a blob still opens immediately, but each step down lowers storage cost and raises access cost. The archive tier is offline and has the lowest storage cost, with a 180-day minimum: before an archived blob can be read it must be rehydrated to an online tier, which can take hours. Removing data from a cooler tier before its minimum period ends causes an early deletion charge. A lifecycle management policy can move blobs to cooler tiers or delete them automatically, for example to cool after 30 days and to archive after 180 days.

concepts.heading: Azure Data Lake Storage and the Hierarchical Namespace
concepts.body: Azure Data Lake Storage is not a separate service or account type. It is a set of big data analytics capabilities built on Blob Storage, switched on by enabling the hierarchical namespace on a storage account; older material calls it Data Lake Storage Gen2. In a flat blob namespace, folders are only name prefixes such as sales/2026/10/file.csv, so renaming a folder means processing every blob under it. With the hierarchical namespace, directories are real objects: renaming or deleting a directory is one atomic metadata operation, and you can set POSIX-style access control lists on directories and files in addition to Azure RBAC. Analytics engines such as Apache Spark reach the data through the Hadoop-compatible ABFS driver. Because the data is still stored as blobs, you keep Blob Storage features such as access tiers and lifecycle management. A scenario about Spark over petabytes of raw files organized in folders points to Data Lake Storage.

concepts.heading: Azure Files and Azure Table Storage
concepts.body: Azure Files provides fully managed file shares in the cloud. SMB shares can be mounted at the same time by Windows, Linux and macOS clients, in Azure or on premises, which makes them the usual way to replace an on-premises file server without changing the applications that map a drive. NFS shares serve Linux workloads, and each share uses one protocol. Azure File Sync can cache Azure file shares on Windows Servers, so branch offices read frequently used files locally while the full share lives in Azure. Azure Table storage is a NoSQL key-attribute store for structured, non-relational data. Each entity is a set of name-value properties, entities in one table do not need the same columns, and each entity is identified by a partition key plus a row key that is unique within the partition. Entities with the same partition key can be queried faster and updated atomically. If a Table storage app later needs global distribution and indexes on every property, Azure Cosmos DB for Table keeps the same programming model.

examPoints: A scenario that describes photos, video or backups served by URL is testing Blob Storage, while one that describes a shared drive that many PCs map at once is testing Azure Files.

A question about access tiers is usually testing three facts: cool, cold and archive trade lower storage cost for higher access cost, archive is offline and needs rehydration, and tiers apply only to block blobs.

A question that mentions directories, ACLs on folders, Spark or big data analytics over a storage account is testing Azure Data Lake Storage, which is Blob Storage with the hierarchical namespace enabled.

quiz.q: A company keeps scanned contracts in Azure Blob Storage. After the first year they are almost never opened, but when a lawyer asks for one it must be readable at once. Which tier lowers storage cost while meeting this need?
choices: Archive tier, because it has the lowest storage cost and each scan can be read as soon as it is requested
Hot tier, because it has the lowest access cost and keeps every scan readable as soon as it is requested
Cold tier, because it is online, suits rarely read data and each scan can be read as soon as it is requested
Page blob storage, because page blobs keep large scanned files cheaper than any block blob access tier can
quiz.explain: The cold tier is online, so a contract opens immediately, and it is designed for rarely accessed data with a lower storage cost than hot or cool. Choice A is tempting because archive has the lowest storage cost of all, but archived blobs are offline and must be rehydrated for hours before they can be read, which breaks the at-once requirement.

quiz.q: A team stores raw clickstream files in a storage account and wants real directories that can be renamed in one operation and folder-level permissions for Spark jobs. What should it do?
choices: Enable the hierarchical namespace on the storage account so that it gains Azure Data Lake Storage capabilities
Create an Azure Files NFS share for the clickstream files so that Linux Spark clusters can mount the folders
Store the clickstream files as append blobs so that each folder can be renamed and secured as a single unit
Move the clickstream files into Azure Table storage and use the partition key as the name of each folder
quiz.explain: Enabling the hierarchical namespace turns a storage account into Azure Data Lake Storage, which adds real directories with atomic rename and delete, POSIX-style ACLs on folders and files, and ABFS access for Spark. Choice B is tempting because NFS shares do have folders and serve Linux clients, but Azure Files is a file-share service, not the Blob-based data lake that analytics engines are built to use.

days.recap: Blob Storage keeps unstructured objects in containers as block, page or append blobs; block blobs can use hot, cool, cold or offline archive tiers; the hierarchical namespace turns Blob Storage into Data Lake Storage; Azure Files serves SMB and NFS shares; Table storage is a cheap NoSQL key-attribute store.

days.title: Azure Cosmos DB: Global Distribution, Consistency, Request Units, and APIs
services: Azure Cosmos DB for Apache Cassandra
Azure Cosmos DB for Apache Gremlin

concepts.heading: What Azure Cosmos DB Is For
concepts.body: Azure Cosmos DB is a fully managed, globally distributed NoSQL database delivered as platform as a service, so Microsoft handles provisioning, patching, updates and backups. Data is organized as account, then database, then container, then item. The container is the unit of storage and scaling: you set its partition key, throughput and indexing policy there. Cosmos DB is schema-agnostic, so one item can have five properties and the next fifteen different ones, and by default it indexes every property automatically, so queries work without manual index design. A good partition key has many distinct values and spreads data and requests evenly, for example a customer ID for orders. Typical workloads on Learn are IoT telemetry, gaming, retail catalogs and shopping carts, and web or mobile apps that need low latency at scale. It is not the tool for data warehousing or join-heavy relational apps; for large-scale analytics over Cosmos DB data, Microsoft recommends mirroring it into Microsoft Fabric.

concepts.heading: Global Distribution and Multi-Region Writes
concepts.body: Global distribution is a turnkey feature: you add Azure regions to a Cosmos DB account and the service replicates your data to each of them, so users read from a nearby replica with low latency. By default an account has one write region and any number of read regions. If users far from that write region complain that saving data is slow, you can enable multi-region writes so that each region accepts writes and every user writes to the nearest one. Replicating to several regions also improves availability, because a regional outage does not take the whole database away. For example, a retailer with shoppers on four continents can add a region on each, so shoppers in Seoul and Paris both get fast reads and writes. On the exam, users around the world or a nearby region point to Cosmos DB.

concepts.heading: The Five Consistency Levels
concepts.body: When data is replicated, a read may reach a replica that has not yet received the latest write. Cosmos DB lets you choose how much of that to accept with five consistency levels, from strongest to weakest. Strong guarantees that every read returns the most recent committed write, at the cost of higher write latency. Bounded staleness lets reads lag behind writes by no more than a set number of versions or a set time. Session guarantees that within one client session you always read your own writes, while other sessions may lag a little; Learn calls it the most widely used level. Consistent prefix never shows writes out of order but may return stale data. Eventual gives no ordering guarantee and lets replicas converge over time, the weakest guarantee but the highest availability. For example, a bank balance needs Strong, while a shopping cart where each user must see their own additions fits Session.

concepts.heading: Request Units and Throughput Options
concepts.body: Cosmos DB measures the cost of every database operation in request units, a single performance currency that combines CPU, memory and I/O. Learn describes one request unit as roughly the cost of reading one 1-KB item by its ID and partition key; writes, queries and larger items consume more. You choose how capacity is supplied. Provisioned throughput reserves a number of request units per second on a container or database; with autoscale you set a maximum and Cosmos DB scales between a lower level and that maximum as traffic changes, which suits sudden bursts such as a ticket sale. Serverless has no throughput to provision: you pay only for the request units your operations consume, which fits intermittent, unpredictable traffic with idle hours, but a serverless account runs in a single region. If a scenario needs several regions, it needs provisioned throughput, manual or autoscale.

concepts.heading: Choosing an API
concepts.body: Each Cosmos DB account uses one API, chosen when the account is created; the API decides the data format, query language and client libraries, while all APIs share the same managed storage underneath. Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL is the native API, formerly called the SQL API: it stores JSON documents and is queried with a SQL-like syntax, and it is the default choice for a new app. Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB keeps MongoDB drivers and the MongoDB Query Language and stores BSON documents. Azure Cosmos DB for Table keeps the Azure Table storage programming model and adds global distribution and automatic indexes. Azure Cosmos DB for Apache Cassandra keeps Cassandra drivers and the SQL-like Cassandra Query Language for column-family data. Azure Cosmos DB for Apache Gremlin stores graphs of vertices and edges for queries such as friends of friends. For migrating an existing MongoDB app, Microsoft recommends Azure DocumentDB, a separate service; Azure Cosmos DB for PostgreSQL is on a retirement path, not for new projects.

examPoints: A scenario that pairs flexible-schema data with fast reads and writes for users in many regions is testing Azure Cosmos DB with global distribution, and slow saves far from the write region point to multi-region writes.

A question that describes a read guarantee is testing the consistency levels: latest write always means Strong, read-your-own-writes means Session, and in-order but possibly stale means Consistent prefix.

A question that names existing skills or drivers, such as MongoDB, Cassandra CQL, Table storage SDKs or graph traversals, is testing which Cosmos DB API keeps them, while a brand-new document app points to the NoSQL API.

quiz.q: A news site stores article comments in Azure Cosmos DB across several regions. A reader who posts a comment must see it at once, but other readers may see it a few seconds later. Which consistency level fits with the least extra latency?
choices: Strong, because it makes every reader see each new comment immediately after the write is committed
Eventual, because it keeps latency lowest and still shows each reader their own new comment immediately
Consistent prefix, because it shows comments in order and makes the posting reader see the comment at once
Session, because it lets each reader see their own new comments at once while other readers can lag slightly
quiz.explain: Session consistency guarantees read-your-own-writes within a client session while other sessions may lag a little, which is exactly the requirement, and it costs less latency than Strong. Choice A is tempting because Strong also shows the comment at once, but it does so for every reader and adds write latency that the scenario says is not needed.

quiz.q: A logistics company tracks shipments, warehouses and the routes between them, and its key queries ask which warehouses are reachable from a given port in three hops. Which Azure Cosmos DB API suits this data?
choices: Azure Cosmos DB for Apache Cassandra, which stores each route as a wide row and queries it with CQL
Azure Cosmos DB for Apache Gremlin, which stores vertices and edges and walks them with graph traversals
Azure Cosmos DB for Table, which stores each route as an entity and looks it up by its partition key
Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL, which stores each route as a JSON document and queries it with joins
quiz.explain: Multi-hop relationship queries over things and the links between them are what a graph database is for, and Azure Cosmos DB for Apache Gremlin stores vertices and edges and queries them with Gremlin traversals. Choice D is tempting because the NoSQL API is the general-purpose default, but its JOIN works only within a single document, so walking many hops across documents is not what it is built for.

days.recap: Azure Cosmos DB is a fully managed, schema-agnostic, globally distributed NoSQL database; add regions and multi-region writes for global users, pick one of five consistency levels (Session is the most widely used), size capacity in request units with provisioned, autoscale or serverless throughput, and choose one API per account: NoSQL, MongoDB, Table, Cassandra or Gremlin.

days.title: Large-Scale Analytics I: ETL and ELT, Warehouses, Lakes, Lakehouses, Delta, and OneLake

concepts.heading: The Parts of an Analytics Solution
concepts.body: Large-scale analytics solutions share four common elements. Data ingestion and processing copies data from transactional databases, files, applications and other sources into an analytical store, and cleans, filters and reshapes it on the way. The analytical data store holds the prepared data, usually a relational data warehouse, a data lake, or a lakehouse that combines them. An analytical data model, today usually a semantic model, describes tables, relationships, hierarchies and measures so that analysts can build reports without writing complex queries against the store. Data visualization, such as Power BI reports and dashboards, presents the results to decision makers. For example, a retailer copies each night's orders from its sales database into a warehouse, a semantic model defines total revenue by product and region, and managers view it in a report. On the exam, match each element to its job: ingestion moves data, the store keeps it, the model describes it, visualization shows it.

concepts.heading: ETL Versus ELT
concepts.body: Extract, transform, load (ETL) reads data from the source, transforms it on a separate processing engine, and only then loads the clean result into the analytical store. Extract, load, transform (ELT) loads the raw data into the target first and transforms it there, using the compute power of the target itself. ETL suits targets with limited processing capacity and cases where an audited staging step must clean or mask data before it reaches the store, for example removing personal data before a reporting database ever sees it. ELT suits modern lakehouses and cloud warehouses with elastic compute, handles large data volumes without extra copy steps, and keeps the untouched raw data so it can be transformed again later for analyses nobody has planned yet. On the exam, a phrase such as transformed before it is loaded means ETL, while load the raw data first and transform it in the store means ELT.

concepts.heading: Pipelines and Ingestion Tools
concepts.body: A pipeline orchestrates the activities that move and transform data: copy data from a source, run a stored procedure, run a notebook, then repeat on a schedule, with steps in sequence or in parallel and with retries when a step fails. Inside Microsoft Fabric, pipelines belong to the Data Factory workload, which also offers Dataflow Gen2, a low-code, Power Query-based tool for analysts who want to merge, clean and reshape data without writing code. Engineers who need custom logic, such as calling a REST API that has no connector, use a Spark notebook in PySpark, Scala, R or SQL. Outside Fabric, Azure Data Factory builds data integration pipelines across cloud and on-premises sources, for example copying from on-premises servers into Azure SQL Database. For example, a nightly Fabric pipeline can copy files into a lakehouse, run a notebook that cleans them, and then refresh the tables that reports use.

concepts.heading: Warehouses, Lakes, and Lakehouses
concepts.body: A data warehouse is a relational database optimized for analytical queries rather than transactions. Its data is usually organized as a star schema of fact tables, such as sales, surrounded by dimension tables, such as product, customer and date, and analysts query it with SQL. A data lake stores large volumes of files in their native formats, structured, semi-structured and unstructured, on distributed storage such as Azure Data Lake Storage; it is flexible and cheap at scale, but plain files lack table features. A data lakehouse combines the two: data stays as files in the lake, and a table layer on top lets analysts query those files with SQL as if they were warehouse tables. Choose a warehouse for structured, SQL-first BI reporting, a lake for raw and varied data that data scientists explore, and a lakehouse when you want lake flexibility and warehouse-style querying over one copy of the data.

concepts.heading: Delta Lake and OneLake
concepts.body: Delta Lake is the open table format that makes a lakehouse work. A Delta table is a set of Parquet data files plus a transaction log, and that log adds what plain files lack: ACID transactions so a failed write never leaves half a table, schema enforcement so bad rows are rejected, and versioning so you can query earlier versions of a table. Both Microsoft Fabric and Azure Databricks store lakehouse tables in Delta format. OneLake is the single, tenant-wide, logical data lake for Microsoft Fabric, often compared to OneDrive for data. Every Fabric tenant gets exactly one OneLake automatically, with no storage account to create, and it is built on Azure Data Lake Storage. Every Fabric engine, such as Spark, the SQL engine of the warehouse, and Power BI, reads and writes the same Delta tables in OneLake, so a table loaded by one team can be used by another without copying or exporting it.

examPoints: A scenario that says data is cleaned on a separate engine before it reaches the store is testing ETL, while one that keeps raw data and transforms it inside an elastic lakehouse or warehouse is testing ELT.
A question that contrasts relational SQL tables, raw files in many formats, and files queried as tables is testing data warehouse versus data lake versus data lakehouse.

A question about ACID transactions, schema enforcement or versioning on Parquet files is testing Delta Lake, and one about a single automatic, tenant-wide lake shared by every Fabric engine is testing OneLake.

quiz.q: A company loads all raw sensor files into its Fabric lakehouse first and runs Spark jobs there to clean and aggregate them, keeping the raw files for future analyses. What kind of process is this?
choices: ELT, because the raw data is loaded into the target first and transformed there using the target's own compute
ETL, because the data is transformed on a separate engine and only the clean result is loaded into the target
OLTP, because the sensor files are written row by row into the lakehouse as each individual reading arrives
Mirroring, because the raw sensor files are copied into OneLake unchanged and kept in step with their source
quiz.explain: Loading raw data into the lakehouse first and transforming it there with the lakehouse's Spark compute is extract, load, transform, and keeping the raw files is a typical ELT benefit. Choice B is tempting because the data does get transformed, but in ETL the transformation happens before loading, on a separate engine, and the raw data would not be kept in the target.

quiz.q: A data engineer accidentally overwrites a lakehouse table with bad data and needs to see what the table looked like yesterday. Which capability of the Delta format makes this possible?
choices: The Parquet files themselves, which keep a full copy of every earlier row inside each newly written file
The semantic model, which keeps each daily refresh of the table in memory as a separate cached version
The transaction log, which records every change so that earlier versions of the table can be queried
The OneLake shortcut, which keeps a separate copy of each table version in a linked external storage account
quiz.explain: A Delta table is Parquet files plus a transaction log, and that log records every change, which is what lets you query earlier versions of a table. Choice A is tempting because Parquet holds the actual data, but plain Parquet files have no history; versioning comes from the Delta transaction log on top of them.

days.recap: Analytics solutions ingest, store, model and visualize data; ETL transforms before loading and ELT transforms inside the target; warehouses hold relational star schemas, lakes hold raw files, and lakehouses query lake files as tables; Delta Lake adds ACID, schema enforcement and versions to Parquet, and OneLake is Fabric's one tenant-wide lake.

days.title: Large-Scale Analytics II: Microsoft Fabric Workloads and Azure Databricks

concepts.heading: Microsoft Fabric as One SaaS Platform
concepts.body: Microsoft Fabric is a unified analytics platform delivered as software as a service, so there are no servers, clusters or storage accounts to provision. All of its workloads share OneLake as storage and Delta Lake as the table format. The workloads include Data Factory for data integration, Data Engineering for Spark and lakehouses, Data Warehouse for T-SQL warehousing, Data Science for machine learning, Real-Time Intelligence for streaming data, and Power BI for reports. Each team works in workspaces that hold items such as lakehouses, warehouses, pipelines, notebooks and reports. Because every item reads and writes the same OneLake data, a data engineer can build a table that a SQL analyst and a Power BI report then use without anyone copying it. Learn's current DP-900 module teaches Microsoft Fabric and Azure Databricks as the two main platforms for large-scale analytics on Azure; older material also covers Azure Synapse Analytics, but focus on Fabric and Databricks for this exam.

concepts.heading: Lakehouse Versus Warehouse in Fabric
concepts.body: A Fabric lakehouse stores structured, semi-structured and unstructured data as files and Delta tables in OneLake, and data engineers and data scientists work with it mainly through Spark notebooks. Every lakehouse also gets a SQL analytics endpoint, which lets analysts query its Delta tables with T-SQL, but that endpoint is read-only: SELECT works, while INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE do not. A Fabric warehouse is the SQL-first option: it supports full T-SQL, including writes and transactions that update several tables at once, and suits curated data modeled as a star schema for BI reporting.
